source.title: Cosine Similarity Is Not Evidence: Measuring the Noise Floor of Interpretability Transfer Under Quantization

page_placements.theme: Direction estimation: sensitivity to prompt sets, baselines, labels, layer, normalisation and outlier channels, and estimator reliability

record.tranche_reason: The study reuses the difference-in-means refusal direction and directional ablation/addition, and tests them after simulated quantization. Its own-null cosine measurement and behavioral interventions test transfer to quantized variants, although behavioral rates are withheld.
record.gate_note: Section 5 measures cross-precision direction cosine against within-model split-half nulls. Appendix D reports qualitative outcomes for directional ablation and addition, but withholds refusal rates because the substring classifier has unmeasured agreement with human judgment. The Monte Carlo floor validation and constructed AUROC/translation experiments do not test the listed versions. The paper's transfer setting is simulated quantization of Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct.
record.test_reason: The study applies Arditi et al.'s difference-in-means direction, directional ablation and activation addition to simulated INT8/INT4 copies of Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, a new setting. It reports cross-precision direction cosines against within-model nulls and qualitative behavioral outcomes of FP16-derived interventions on the quantized copies. This bears on V6 (transfer to quantized variants) and on V1 in this model. It is not an original source. It is better classed as a new setting (T3) than a same-method replication (T1), because the headline measure is cross-precision cosine rather than refusal rates.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The paper's central conclusion is methodological: cosines between estimated directions are not evidence of preservation without the estimator's noise floor. A published cross-precision cosine of 0.996 is uninterpretable without its n. Against each bit-width's own null, the refusal direction rotated at INT4, while INT8 shows no detected movement (explicitly not equivalence). Qualitatively, FP16-direction ablation suppresses refusal at all tested bit-widths, and add_relative works only at c=1 (zero at c=4). Behavioral rates are withheld because the substring classifier is unvalidated.
record.recipe_differences: Uses the difference-in-means refusal direction and directional ablation/addition, but tests simulated group-wise asymmetric quantization of one instruct model. Behavioral effects are headroom-normalized and numerical rates are withheld; the cross-precision cosine is judged against a within-quantized-model split-half null.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome varies with bit-width: INT8 is within noise, whereas INT4 shows rotation. Add_relative also varies sharply with coefficient: c=1 induces refusal on harmless prompts, while c=4 yields zero.

fits_no_version.finding: On real Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct activations, split-half cosine floors of the difference-in-means estimator are 0.979–0.994 across six layers at n=256, matching the closed form (1+4/κ)^-1 within 0.0008.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Similarity between estimated refusal directions must be read against the estimator's sampling noise floor (κ = nρ²/d). Otherwise high cosines, such as a published 0.996 across precision, are uninterpretable.

fits_no_version.finding: In constructed experiments (n=1200, d=64), pure translation of a probe's score leaves AUROC unchanged while accuracy falls from 0.735 to 0.550; attenuation moves AUROC by up to 0.13.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Scale-invariant statistics cannot distinguish translation from attenuation of a transferred decision variable.

record.problems: The behavioral refusal rates are withheld; the substring refusal classifier has no measured agreement with human judgment. The five seeds resample fit/evaluation splits from the same 520 prompts rather than providing independent replications. Quantization is simulated and weight-only. Output quality and retained general capability were not measured. The authors describe the Table 3 decision rule as conservative, not a calibrated test.
record.rows_left_out: No other claim-version behavioral results were omitted. Section 3 and Appendix A's Monte Carlo validation of the floor formula, Table 2's extrapolation to a published cosine, and Appendix C's constructed translation/attenuation experiments do not directly test the listed claim versions. Appendix D's withheld numerical rates cannot be recorded as numbers; its explicit qualitative outcomes are in R3-R5.

untested.parts: Preservation of other abilities and output quality was not measured. There are no numerical refusal rates, and complete removal of refusal is not shown.

Not tested: transfer across languages, base-to-instruct transfer, other model families or sizes, real (non-simulated) quantization kernels, and activation quantization. Behavioral transfer has no numerical rates or equivalence test.

missing.what: add_absolute over the same coefficient sweep is monotone with no cliff. This contrasts with add_relative and shows the c=4 zero is operator-specific.
Subspace gain |hq·v|/|hfp·v| is 1.007 at INT8 and 0.933 at INT4, a projection-magnitude change along the refusal direction under quantization.
Repaired harmless-prompt refusal baseline of 0.05 (pilot 0.375 before loader fix), needed as the baseline for R4/R5.

record.verdict_notes: Treating quantized copies as 'model variants' under V6 is an interpretive choice. Researchers may judge this a narrower transfer setting than the version intends. The INT4 result was relabelled from challenges to limits_scope: similarity stays at 0.96 and the FP16 direction still ablates refusal there. Behavioral rows rest on qualitative statements only. The five seeds are resampled splits of the same 520 prompts, not independent replications.

versions.untested_parts: Whether the intervention preserves other abilities was not measured. The behavioral arm gives no numerical refusal rates, and ablation is reported as suppressing only a large fraction of available headroom rather than eliminating refusal.
No practical weight edit or released-model abliteration is tested.
No jailbreak mechanism or training against ablation is tested.
The study does not test whether refusal is carried by multiple directions, an affine structure, or a cone.
No separation of harmfulness judgment from refusal decision is tested.
Transfer is tested only under simulated quantization of one instruct model, not across languages, base-to-instruct stages, or other model families.
No refusal-training schedule or training-stage comparison is tested.

rows.measure: Cosine of quantized direction to FP16 direction
rows.note: The cross-precision cosine is below the within-INT4 null by more than twice the null's split-to-split spread.
rows.check: State 'reversed' is wrong. A cosine of 0.9647 to the FP16 direction is still high similarity. The authors detect a small rotation beyond the INT4 estimator's own noise (own null 0.9803 − 2×0.0052), not an opposite or lost direction. Table 3 also gives INT4 subspace gain 0.933. In Appendix D, FP16-direction ablation still suppresses refusal at every bit-width.

rows.check: State 'reversed' is wrong. At c=4, add_relative fails to induce refusal: the rate is exactly zero, against a harmless baseline of about 0.05. That is no induction, not an opposite effect. The authors note it may reflect degenerate generation, since output quality was not measured. add_absolute over the same sweep is monotone with no cliff, so the failure is specific to the add_relative operator. Baseline should read about 0.05, the repaired harmless baseline (Appendix E), not 'not stated'.

relation.reason: Its own cross-precision cosines against within-model nulls, and qualitative ablation/addition outcomes, bear on V6 and V1.

tranche.reason: Applies Arditi et al.'s DIM direction, ablation and addition to a new setting (simulated quantized copies), with results on transfer. Its methodological critique is aimed at another study's evidence, not at the version itself, so it isn't T5.

source_check.notes: All behavioural results are qualitative: rates from 45,000 completions are withheld (substring classifier unvalidated, no TOST, output quality not measured). The cited 0.996 cosine is Chhabra & Khalili's, not this study's. The text doesn't state the layer for Table 3; its floor uses layer-16 rho. Harmless refusal baseline is 0.05 after the loader repair (App. E).

statements.correction: add_relative c=1: harmless refusal near baseline to near ceiling. c=4: exactly zero in every bit-width and seed. add_absolute is monotone with no cliff. Output quality wasn't measured, so zero may be degenerate generation. Rates are withheld.
statements.problem: The part on this study is right. It leaves out the authors' caveats.

statements.correction: INT8 cos 0.9999 vs own null 0.9827 (sd 0.0047). Authors: 'no detected movement', not an equivalence claim. Smallest detectable deficit 0.0104. Ablation suppresses refusal at every bit-width tested (qualitative). Repo: github.com/pvarshh/quantinterp (footnote 1).
statements.problem: Numbers right (0.9999, own null 0.9827, 200 splits). The c=1 effect isn't stated per bit-width. The text names github.com/pvarshh/quantinterp as its own repo, so 'looks like the same work' is too weak.

statements.correction: INT4 cos 0.9647 vs own null 0.9803 (sd 0.0052). Threshold 0.9803 - 2(0.0052) = 0.9699 is in the Table 3 caption. Simulated, weight-only quantization.
statements.problem: Right for this study. The n/2 value 0.9640 isn't in this paper's text; it comes from the gh record.
